# Magnetic variation (declination) and deviation (`magnetic_declination`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: needs magnetic_compass; helped by map_projection_charts, dead_reckoning_log_line
- Core idea: The needle aligns with the local horizontal magnetic field. At each place it is off true north by an angle (variation) that differs from place to place and slowly changes over the years. Measure it by comparing the compass with the true north given by the Pole Star or by the Sun's bearing at rising and setting (the bisector of equal-altitude bearings defines the meridian), then correct every course; a few degrees uncorrected over a 5,000 km crossing puts you hundreds of kilometres off. Iron aboard adds its own error (deviation), which changes with the ship's heading.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming variation is fixed forever; it drifts several degrees per century (Gellibrand 1635)
  - Hoping to find longitude from variation, a 16th–18th c. dream that never worked reliably
  - Correcting in the wrong direction (after correcting shipboard deviation, add easterly variation to a magnetic bearing to obtain true bearing)
- History: china: 1088 – Shen Kuo notes the needle points slightly east of south; europe: 15th c. – Nuremberg portable sundials mark the local declination; 13–17 Sept 1492 Columbus notices the variation change in mid-Atlantic; 1538–41 João de Castro measures it systematically; 1635 Gellibrand shows secular change; 1701 Halley's isogonic chart; c. 1801–03 Flinders studies ship's iron deviation
- Read:
  - Edmond Halley, A New and Correct Chart Shewing the Variations of the Compass in the Western & Southern Oceans (1701)
  - E. G. R. Taylor, The Haven-Finding Art: A History of Navigation from Odysseus to Captain Cook (1956)
